blocks.text: Now that what version control is and why it matters are established, the next question is architectural: where does the history actually live, and who has access to all of it? Version control systems fall into three broad models based on the answer, local, centralized, and distributed, and understanding all three makes it clear exactly what Git's design choice buys you.

These three models are not just historical trivia. They represent three genuinely different answers to the same question, and the tradeoffs each one makes (collaboration ability, offline capability, resilience to failure) show up directly in day-to-day Git usage later in this course.

blocks.alt: The three version control models side by side
blocks.caption: Local, centralized, and distributed VCS differ in where the full history is allowed to live.

blocks.text: 1. Local Version Control

The earliest approach to version control kept everything on a single machine. A simple local tool maintains a patch database, a record of the differences between successive versions of a file, right next to the files themselves. To recover an old version, the tool replays the recorded patches in sequence from the earliest version up to the one you want.

blocks.alt: A local version control system on one machine
blocks.caption: Local VCS keeps history as a patch database on the same machine as the files, with no other copy anywhere.

blocks.text:
This solves the "more than one point in time" problem from a single machine, but does nothing for collaboration, and carries an obvious risk: if that machine's disk is lost or corrupted, the history is lost along with it.
Local VCS is largely historical today (tools like RCS and SCCS from the 1970s and 1980s), rarely used in real projects now, but understanding it clarifies what centralized and distributed systems each add on top.

blocks.alt: How a local VCS reconstructs a version from patches
blocks.caption: Each version is derived by applying a stored patch to the previous one, all on one machine.

code.content:
# Conceptually, what a local VCS like RCS does under the hood
rcs -i document.txt        # initialize version tracking for one file
ci document.txt             # check in a new revision (records a patch)
co -r1.2 document.txt        # check out revision 1.2 by replaying patches

blocks.title: Why this is mostly historical
blocks.content: Local VCS is rarely something you would choose to use today. It is covered here because centralized and distributed systems are best understood as direct responses to its two biggest gaps: no built-in collaboration, and no resilience if the one machine holding the history is lost.

blocks.title: A file-by-file model
blocks.content: Early local tools like RCS typically tracked one file at a time rather than a whole project as a single unit. That per-file granularity is itself something later models moved away from: Git, as later topics cover, snapshots the entire project together at every commit, not individual files independently.

blocks.title: Using Git with no remote is not Local VCS
blocks.content: Running git init and only ever committing locally, with no remote configured, might look similar to a local VCS on the surface. It is not the same thing architecturally: the repository is still fully distributed in capability (it can be cloned, pushed, and merged with any other Git repository at any time), you are simply choosing, for now, not to use that capability. A true local VCS has no such option built in.

blocks.text: 2. Centralized Version Control

Centralized version control systems (CVCS), such as SVN (Subversion) and the older CVS, solve the collaboration gap by introducing one central server that holds the full history. Developers check out a working copy from that server, make changes, and commit directly back to it. Everyone sees a single, authoritative history.

blocks.caption: Every developer talks to one central server, which is the only place the full history lives.

blocks.text:
This is a real improvement over local VCS: multiple people can now work on the same project with a shared, coordinated history. But it introduces a new problem: the central server is a single point of failure.
If it goes down, is unreachable, or is lost without a separate backup, nobody can commit, and in many CVCS designs nobody can even view the full history, since working copies typically only hold the current checked-out version, not the entire history.

blocks.alt: What happens when the central server in a CVCS fails
blocks.caption: A centralized model ties every commit and most history access to one server being available.

code.content:
# Centralized-style workflow (SVN)
svn checkout https://svn.example.com/project/trunk   # get a working copy
# ... edit files ...
svn commit -m "Fix login bug"                          # goes straight to the central server
svn update                                             # pull others' changes from the server

blocks.text: 3. Distributed Version Control

Distributed version control systems (DVCS), of which Git is the dominant example, remove the single point of failure by giving every clone the full history, not just the current files. When you git clone a repository, you get every commit that has ever been made, not a partial view.

blocks.caption: Every clone in a DVCS carries the complete history, making every developer a full peer rather than a thin client.

blocks.text: This means you can commit, browse history, create branches, and inspect any past version entirely offline, since none of that requires talking to a server. A remote (commonly a shared server like GitHub) is still used by convention to synchronize work between people, but technically it is just another peer with a full copy, not a uniquely privileged source of truth the way a CVCS server is. This distinction is explored in depth in the next topic.

code.content:
# Distributed-style workflow (Git)
git clone https://github.com/team/project.git   # get the ENTIRE history, not just current files
git log --oneline                                # browse full history, works offline
git commit -m "Fix login bug"                     # commits locally first, no server needed
git push origin main                              # sync local history to the shared remote

blocks.title: Every clone is a full backup
blocks.content: Because a DVCS clone contains the complete history, every developer's laptop is, incidentally, a full backup of the project. This is a direct consequence of the model, not a bolted-on feature, and is exactly the mechanism behind the disaster recovery benefit covered in the previous topic.

blocks.text: One quiet consequence of the distributed model is worth flagging early, since it explains why branching feels so cheap in Git compared to older systems: a branch is just a small pointer stored locally, not a separate area on a shared server that has to be provisioned or synchronized. Branching is covered in full in the Branching module, but the reason it is nearly instant traces directly back to the distributed model described here.
4. Locking vs Merging: A Deeper Difference

Beyond where history lives, centralized and distributed systems often differ in how they handle two people touching the same file. Some centralized systems lean on a lock-modify-unlock model: a developer locks a file before editing it, preventing anyone else from changing it until the lock is released.

Git's model is copy-modify-merge: every developer edits their own full copy freely and simultaneously, and conflicting edits are reconciled at merge time rather than prevented up front. This trades a small amount of merge overhead for much greater parallelism, nobody is ever blocked waiting on someone else to finish.

blocks.caption: Locking prevents simultaneous edits; merging allows them and reconciles differences afterward.

blocks.title: Common pitfall
blocks.content: Locking feels safer at first glance (no conflicts possible), but it does not scale: real teams end up waiting on each other constantly, especially on frequently touched files. Copy-modify-merge is what actually enables the "many people working in parallel" benefit covered in the previous topic on why version control matters.

blocks.text: 5. Choosing a Model Today

In practice, this decision has largely already been made for you: distributed, and specifically Git, is the default choice for new projects across the industry, for reasons the coming topics (Why Companies Use Git in particular) cover in depth. Local VCS is essentially never chosen deliberately today. Centralized VCS still appears, mostly in older enterprises with deep, long-standing SVN investments.

blocks.alt: A decision flow for choosing a version control model
blocks.caption: In practice almost every path leads to a distributed VCS like Git for new projects today.

items: Local: effectively obsolete for real projects, of historical and educational interest only.
Centralized: occasionally still found in legacy enterprise environments already built around SVN.
Distributed: the default for essentially all new software projects, open source and commercial alike.

blocks.text: 6. Hybrid and Enterprise Variants

Real-world version control is not always a clean fit into exactly one of these three boxes. Some tools blend ideas from more than one model to fit a specific niche, and it is worth knowing they exist so the three-model picture does not feel artificially tidy.

Perforce (Helix Core), common in game studios and large enterprises with huge binary assets, is architecturally centralized (one authoritative server) but gives each developer a local workspace cache for speed, closer to a centralized system with performance optimizations than a true DVCS. Team Foundation Version Control (TFVC), from Microsoft's older tooling, is similarly centralized and still lingers in some enterprise shops that have not migrated to Git.

blocks.title: Why this matters practically
blocks.content: If you join a team using Perforce or TFVC, do not assume Git-style instincts (cheap local branches, fully offline commits, every clone as a full backup) transfer directly. Those tools inherit the centralized model's tradeoffs even where they add local caching for speed.

blocks.text: 7. Comparing All Three Models

blocks.title: Real scenario
blocks.content: A developer is on a long flight with no internet access. On a centralized system, they effectively cannot commit or meaningfully browse history until they land. On a distributed system like Git, they can commit freely, create branches, review the entire project history, and simply push everything to the remote once they are back online.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
points: Local VCS keeps a patch history on one machine; it solves recall over time but not collaboration or resilience, and is largely historical today.

Centralized VCS (SVN, CVS) adds a shared central server so teams can collaborate, but that server becomes a single point of failure, and some CVCS tools further restrict parallelism with file locking.

Distributed VCS (Git, Mercurial) gives every clone the full history, enabling full offline work, removing the single-server risk, and enabling a copy-modify-merge model that scales to large, parallel teams.
The next topic goes deeper on centralized versus distributed specifically, including how distributed systems still use a conventional "central" remote in practice.
